source: Zhu et al. (2023) Large Language Models can Learn Rules (Hypotheses-to-Theories)
finding: HtT has the LLM induce rules on training examples, keeps rules that are often used and often right, and puts that rule library in the prompt at test time. It lifts accuracy a lot on relational, numeric and list tasks.
numbers: Abstract: absolute gain 10-30%. Symbolic CLUTRR (kinship), average over 2-10 hops: GPT-4 5-shot CoT 50.6 -> 64.3 with HtT (+13.7); GPT-3.5 CoT 21.2 -> 37.6 (+16.4); GPT-3.5 with rules induced by GPT-4 reached 48.4 (+27.2). Supervised EdgeTransformer 71.8.
quote: prompting methods that rely on implicit knowledge in an LLM often generate incorrect answers when the implicit knowledge is wrong
limits: Rules induced from labelled training questions. Prompt tags mattered (GPT-4: 1 tag 59.6, 2 tags 64.3). Gain on GPT-3.5 for textual CLUTRR was not significant because it makes other errors.
agent_relevance: Matches S2/S3: induce a rule library with counts of use and of correct use, then retrieve rules at solve time. Keep the library under code control.

source: Zhu et al. (2023) Large Language Models can Learn Rules (Hypotheses-to-Theories) - random-rule control
finding: Replacing the conclusions of learned rules with random answers hurts a lot, so the gain comes from correct rules, not just from showing the format of a rule.
numbers: GPT-4 CLUTRR average: 5-shot CoT 50.6; with random rules 9.9 (-40.7); HtT unsorted 57.1, sorted 60.0.
limits: Min et al. 2022 found random labels matter little for simple classification; the authors say multi-step reasoning differs. One model, one task.
agent_relevance: A wrong rule in the prompt is worse than no rule. Any rule shown to the model must have passed a held-out check (G3).

source: Zhu et al. (2023) Large Language Models can Learn Rules (Hypotheses-to-Theories) - error analysis
finding: Most CoT errors on rule-based tasks come from the model recalling a wrong rule, not from bad chaining.
numbers: Incorrect rules cause 65% of CoT errors on CLUTRR and 81% on base-16 arithmetic (manual analysis). Base-16 library from GPT-4: precision 98.5%, recall 92.2%. List Functions: HtT gave +18.5 to +18.7 raw accuracy and +10.2 to +14.5 task accuracy over 4-shot CoT (GPT-4 task accuracy 46.0 -> 56.2).
limits: Manual analysis on a small sample; arithmetic bases are synthetic.
agent_relevance: Supports S2: the main failure to fix is a wrong remembered rule. A verified rule store is a direct fix.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning of LMs with hypothesis refinement (ICLR)
finding: Propose rules, test them with a symbolic interpreter, refine. LMs are good at proposing candidate rules when a program checks them, but poor at applying their own rules.
numbers: GPT-4. Task accuracy IO vs refinement (T=3, N=5): ACRE 28.0 -> 59.0; MiniSCAN 0.0 -> 46.0 (T=3, N=1; higher with more samples); List Functions 39.6 (IO) vs about 52; MiniARC raw accuracy was worse than IO (33.1 vs 18.7).
limits: Interpreter is task-specific. MiniARC is text-only 5x5 grids and refinement lagged IO there. The results table in the PDF text is garbled, so the exact cell mapping for some rows is approximate.
agent_relevance: Strong support for S2/S3: the LLM proposes, code verifies. Do not trust the LLM to apply the rule it wrote.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning of LMs with hypothesis refinement (ICLR) - induction vs application gap
finding: When the LM itself applies the rules it proposed, accuracy collapses compared with a symbolic interpreter applying them.
numbers: Task accuracy on MiniSCAN dropped from more than 80% to almost zero when the LM applied the rules.
limits: Authors note LMs are known to be weak on symbolic execution; they do not claim equal performance is expected.
agent_relevance: Rule application must be done by code or a tool, not by free-text reasoning. Fits the principle that code selects.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning of LMs with hypothesis refinement (ICLR) - noise and humans
finding: LM rule induction is brittle to a few wrong examples, more than humans. LM rules are often better than human rules on List Functions, but worse on MiniARC where humans give short analogy-based descriptions.
numbers: Perturbing 12.5%, 25%, 50% of 8 exemplars: performance dropped even with one noisy example and fell steadily; telling the LM about noise reduced but did not remove the drop. Human study on 50 tasks per dataset: relative drop with noise larger for the LM.
limits: Human study small and not run on all conditions (authors say so). Perturbation might make some tasks ill-posed.
agent_relevance: Noisy examples are a real risk for S2 candidate rules. Plan tolerant scoring (cover most, not all) rather than all-or-nothing fit.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR)
finding: Generate many natural-language hypotheses, then code each as a Python program and run it on the examples. This beats direct output prediction on ARC and other induction tasks.
numbers: GPT-4, 100 random ARC tasks, top-1: direct 17%, program only 23%, LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected hypotheses 33%, human-written (LARC) hypotheses 45%. Non-LM DSL system Icecuber 43%. 1D-ARC: direct 39.6, program only 61.1, full 73.1. SyGuS (89 tasks): CrossBeam 74.8, GPT-4 94.3. List Functions (100 tasks): direct 31, program only 59, full 69.
limits: GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 of 100 ARC tasks (human check); 28 of the 30 solved had a correct hypothesis before summarising. 64 hypotheses plus 3 rounds of execution feedback is costly. Top-1 accuracy, not the official top-3.
agent_relevance: Closest published design to S2/S3: abstract hypothesis first, then concrete executable form, then check on examples. The bottleneck is getting the right hypothesis into the pool.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR) - hypothesis vs program bottleneck
finding: Giving a correct human-written hypothesis lifts ARC accuracy to 45%, which shows hypothesis generation, not program writing, is the bottleneck.
numbers: A human-selected hypothesis led to a correct program in 33 of 49 tasks (67%). Low false-positive rate observed.
limits: Human in the loop in two variants; the selected variant is a lower bound.
agent_relevance: Spend budget on diverse candidate rules (S2) and a good selector, not on longer program drafts.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Language Models as Inductive Reasoners (DEER, CoLM)
finding: Induce natural-language rules from natural-language facts instead of formal logic. They build the DEER dataset (1.2k rule-fact pairs) and a pipeline CoLM that generates then filters rules with trained checkers.
numbers: DEER overall correctness 95.5%. GPT-J 6B in-context: raw generator precision 45.0% (recall 100%), CoLM precision 48.1% (recall 72.2%); finetuned CoLM precision 70.0%, recall 54.4%. Filter modules help from 6B parameters up; plateau at 20B.
limits: Old models (GPT-J, GPT-NeoX). METEOR-type metrics correlate weakly with humans (0.29). Filters raise precision but throw away good rules.
agent_relevance: Shows ILP-style goals (rules from facts) can be done in text. Filtering for consistency, reality, generality and non-triviality is a ready checklist for scoring candidate rules in S2.

source: Han et al. (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: On classic property-induction tasks from psychology, GPT-4 matches human patterns for most phenomena. GPT-3.5 does not. Both miss premise non-monotonicity.
numbers: GPT-4 ranking correlation with the Osherson et al. original rankings: Spearman 0.65 (p<0.001). GPT-3.5 beat GPT-4 on General arguments; on single-premise General Mammals arguments GPT-4 was uncorrelated with human ratings. A human similarity-coverage model was best overall.
limits: Blank-property arguments, not rule learning proper. Different model versions may differ.
agent_relevance: Models share human-like inductive habits (similarity, typicality), so the same biases carry into S2 candidates. Do not treat model induction as neutral.

source: Cheng et al. (2024) Inductive or Deductive? Rethinking the fundamental reasoning abilities of LLMs (SolverLearner)
finding: Separating induction (learn y=f(x) as code run by an interpreter) from deduction: GPT-4 induces near perfectly, but is weak at counterfactual deduction.
numbers: GPT-4 via SolverLearner reached accuracy 1 in most cases (arithmetic bases 8/9/10/11/16, syntax orders, spatial coordinate frames, ciphers). GPT-3.5 failed in several cases. Plain zero-shot GPT-3.5 gets base-10 right (about 0.9-1.0) but only about 0.03-0.12 in bases 8, 9, 11.
quote: LLMs demonstrate remarkable inductive reasoning capabilities through SolverLearner
limits: Synthetic tasks with a deterministic function; no noise. Success relies on running the induced code externally. No CoT comparison.
agent_relevance: Supports the split: let the model induce, let code apply. Induction as code beats model-run deduction on out-of-pattern tasks.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining induction and transduction for abstract reasoning
finding: Neural induction (write a program) and transduction (predict the output) solve different ARC tasks. Induction is better at exact computation and composing concepts; transduction at fuzzy perception. Ensembling nears average human level.
numbers: ARC validation, 2 tries: best ensemble 56.75% vs average human 60.2% and best human 97.8%; later work with better test-time training of the transduction model reached 61.9%. Finetuning data quality mattered for induction (18.78% vs 11.07% with 2048 samples) but less for transduction.
limits: Specific to ARC grids with finetuned models; needs both models and large sampling (up to 20k programs).
agent_relevance: Generate rule candidates two ways (a programmatic rule and a direct answer) and compare. Disagreement is a signal (G1). Do not use one mode alone.

source: Cropper and Dumancic (2022) Inductive logic programming at 30: a new introduction (JAIR)
finding: ILP learns readable logic programs from few examples plus background knowledge. Strengths: data efficiency, recursion, predicate invention, reuse. Weaknesses: noise, unstructured input, need for hand-made background knowledge.
numbers: Survey table compares systems on noise, optimality, infinite domains, recursion, predicate invention. States neural methods often need many more examples than symbolic ILP.
limits: Review, no new experiments. Written before LLM-ILP hybrids matured.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for S2/S3 (examples, background knowledge, bias, hypothesis). The weak points are where an LLM could help: noise, raw text, bias choice.

source: Cropper and Morel (2021) Learning programs by learning from failures (Popper)
finding: Generate, test, constrain loop: a failed hypothesis gives constraints that prune the search (too general prunes generalisations; too specific prunes specialisations). Popper beats earlier ILP systems on game, robot and list problems.
numbers: Three domains (toy games, robot strategies, list transformations); compared with Aleph, Metagol, ILASP2i, ILASP3.
limits: No noise handling in the original Popper. Authors warn direct system comparisons are hard because biases differ.
agent_relevance: The loop is almost the same as our test-and-revise loop. Failures should become rules about what to skip, not just a new try (G2, G3).

source: Evans and Grefenstette (2018) Learning explanatory rules from noisy data (dILP)
finding: Differentiable ILP learns logic rules by gradient descent, tolerates mislabelled data, and can sit on top of neural perception.
numbers: At 10% mislabelled data it finds a perfect answer in 5 of 6 tasks; some tasks are fine at 20-30%. Compared with Metagol on 20 symbolic tasks; one task solved in only about 30% of random initialisations.
limits: Needs program templates; small tasks; success depends on random initialisation. Traditional ILP error rises sharply with a single bad label.
agent_relevance: Noise tolerance is the classic ILP gap; a soft score over rule candidates is one design for S2 scoring.

source: Benterki et al. (2026) ALBI: LLM-guided ILP via iterative generate-test-constrain refinement
finding: Replace Popper's ASP generator with an LLM and keep Prolog as the verifier. Three frontier models solve all 30 standard ILP tasks in far fewer iterations than Popper.
numbers: 30 tasks, 100% success for Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6 and Popper. Iterations: ALBI 1.4-1.7 vs Popper 6.8. Time: Popper 81.8 s, Gemini 333.6 s, Claude 397.7 s, GPT 1631.9 s. Clauses 2.7-2.9.
limits: Evaluated only on Popper's own suite with noise-free data, so 100% is a ceiling. LLMs may have seen these benchmarks. Per-iteration cost 10-100 times higher.
agent_relevance: Best direct example of a Popper-style loop with an LLM as hypothesis generator and code as judge. Feed back structured diagnostics (coverage counts, counterexamples).

source: Benterki et al. (2026) ALBI: LLM-guided ILP via iterative generate-test-constrain refinement - anonymisation test
finding: Renaming predicates to p0, p1... does not break induction but makes it slower, so part of the speed comes from word meaning.
numbers: All three models stay at 100% success. Mean iterations rise: Gemini 1.7 -> 2.6, Claude 1.5 -> 2.5, GPT 1.4 -> 1.9 (x1.36-1.67). Tasks needing more than 1 iteration: 40% -> 57%. Hardest, zendo2: 11-17 iterations anonymised vs 1-7.
limits: Same small benchmark. Some models used list notation not allowed in the bias (GPT 9 of 10 program tasks), going beyond the formal language.
agent_relevance: Use a semantic-anonymisation test as a metamorphic check that a learned rule is structural (G3-type).

source: Chen and Ma (2026) Reason Popper-ly: Patching in-context reasoning with inductive logic programming
finding: Learn relation-composition rules with ILP from reasoning traces and use them as a step-level verifier on CoT. The verifier corrects wrong steps and the model continues from the repaired trace.
numbers: CLUTRR, 8-10 hops, terminal accuracy CoT -> Popper-ly: Qwen-3.5 4B 19.09 -> 61.93; Gemma-4 E4B 14.39 -> 62.74; LLaMA-3.2 3B 18.72 -> 42.48; Claude Sonnet 4.6 56.92 -> 71.38; GPT-5.4 59.91 -> 75.09.
limits: One task family (kinship composition) with a small closed rule set. The pure symbolic pipeline was as good or better at short chains. Small models mostly err by wrong rule (43-49%); frontier models by a missing inverse (75-78%).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G2: errors located by code and fixed from real output. A learned rule table is a cheap step checker.

source: Yu et al. (2026) ADVENT: LLM-driven automatic predicate invention for ILP
finding: An LLM invents named helper predicates for ILP (Aleph); Prolog execution results guide refinement; a knowledge pool stores predicates for reuse.
numbers: Nine poker-hand concepts, seven LLMs. ILP alone 0/9 in position-free mode. LLM invention without verification 58%; LLM self-critique 73%; Prolog verification (ADVENT) 80%; ADVENT without knowledge pool 67%. Pool gains up to +31 points (straight flush +31, royal flush +29); flush -9. MiMo 31% -> 93% and DeepSeek 51% -> 87% with verification.
limits: One small domain. Wide confidence intervals per model. Reusing earlier predicates hurt on a simple concept (flush).
agent_relevance: Supports G5 and S3: grounded execution beats self-critique (80 vs 73), and a reusable store of verified concepts helps compositional tasks.

source: Ma et al. (2026) AutoSpec: Safety rule evolution for LLM agents via inductive logic programming
finding: ILP inside an agent loop: from safe/unsafe annotations, find predicates that separate false positives from false negatives, then propose rule edits and verify them (CEGIS).
numbers: 291 traces. Rule F1 0.98 (code execution) and 0.93 (embodied). Up to 94% fewer false positives; 4-5 iterations to converge; up to 4.8x the F1 of a heuristic CEGIS baseline (0.980 vs 0.203 on code execution). Held-out generalisation gaps 1.6% and 4.7%. Users preferred ILP explanations in 84.2% of pairwise comparisons.
limits: Self-built dataset of 291 traces; the initial guardrail scored F1 0.493; user study small.
agent_relevance: A working example of ILP as the rule-learning step in an agent loop. Pattern for our rule library: learn from counterexamples, test on held-out traces.

source: Gandarela et al. (2025) Inductive learning of logical theories with LLMs: an expressivity-graded analysis
finding: LLM plus Prolog feedback is compared with Popper on synthetic theory induction graded by rule structure. Long relation chains hurt LLMs more than rule complexity. More iterations do not reliably help.
numbers: GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Mixtral-8x7B, Llama3-8B vs Popper under noise 0.1-0.3. Larger models: F1 about 0.25 higher than Popper on average, mostly at higher noise. GPT-4o RDG F1 fell from 0.75 (noise 0.1) to 0.22 (noise 0.3). At noise 0.1 GPT-4o F1 was 21 times Llama3-8B. Errors: GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 0% syntactic / 100% logical; Llama3-8B 46% syntactic; Gemma-7B 100% syntactic (no valid Prolog).
limits: Synthetic data; compute not comparable (Popper on CPU). No gain beyond about 3 iterations. Recursive rules removed.
agent_relevance: Cap revision rounds at 3-4. Let code catch syntax errors for weak models.

source: Helff et al. (2026) SLR: Automated synthesis for scalable logical reasoning (SLR-Bench)
finding: Benchmark of 19k inductive tasks in 20 levels with a hidden rule and a validator program. LLMs write valid rules but often wrong ones; reasoning models improve but cost a lot.
numbers: Logical Reasoning Level (0-20): o3 15.5, gpt-5 15.4, o1 11.9, gpt-4o 6.2, Llama-3.3-70B 5.6, Llama-3.1-8B 3.8. Hard-level accuracy: o3 45%, gpt-5 46%, gpt-4o 20%. Syntax score gpt-4o 100%. o3 cost $207 per 1,000 prompts vs $20 for gpt-4o. CoT gains about 5%. Curriculum training roughly doubled Llama-3 8B accuracy.
quote: contemporary LLMs readily produce syntactically valid rules, yet often fail at correct logical inference
limits: Authors' own benchmark; costs at 2025 rates; downstream transfer gains small (about +1 to +6 points).
agent_relevance: Accuracy falls with depth even for strong models; syntax validity is not correctness. Use the validator, not the model, as judge.

source: Li et al. (2024) LLMs for relational reasoning: how far are we?
finding: On ILP relational benchmarks, GPT-4-class models do well on simple concepts and poorly on harder ones. A 60k-parameter neural program-induction model (DLM) beats them.
numbers: GPT-4: 100% on HasFather but 49.05% on IsUncle. DLM scores 100% on most listed tasks. Smaller open models (llama-7b/13b) are near zero on several tasks. Failures include input-conflicting reasoning (saying P8 is both father and mother) and common-sense-conflicting reasoning.
limits: 2024 models. Compare only within this paper's benchmark.
agent_relevance: LLM rule induction degrades with the number of predicates in the target rule. Prefer small search plus a checker over free-form induction for compound relations.

source: Peng et al. (2025) Abductive logical rule induction by bridging ILP and multimodal LLMs (ILP-CoT)
finding: An MLLM proposes the rule structure, ILP (Metagol) builds a pruned task and returns rules over rectified facts. Beats plain prompting.
numbers: CLEVR-Hans (Qwen-7B) test: direct predict 51.60, custom CoT 35.85, ILP-CoT 81.85. ILP backend ablation: Popper 46.74, Metagol 81.85, ILASP out of time. ARC-AGI-1 (400 training tasks), GPT-4o: 5.25% direct, 9.25% custom CoT, 10.25% ILP-CoT.
limits: ARC gains are small (about 5 points); the neural NEUMANN baseline got 97.43 on CLEVR-Hans. Result depends on backend choice.
agent_relevance: LLM-proposed structure plus ILP search cuts the search space. Naive inclusion of all intermediate reasoning in the CoT hurt accuracy.

source: Borroto et al. (2025) Question answering with LLMs and Learning from Answer Sets (LLM2LAS)
finding: An LLM extracts event structure from stories, ILASP learns logic rules, ASP answers questions. Rules are learned, not hand-written.
numbers: bAbI: 100% accuracy on all tasks except task 17 (97.8%); hand-written ASP reaches 100% on all 17 tasks; Mitra and Baral reach 100% except task 16 (93.6%).
limits: bAbI is synthetic and easy; LLM extraction is the weak link.
agent_relevance: Shows ILP can turn LLM-extracted facts into reusable rules; check rules on new stories before use.

source: Rocha et al. (2024) Program synthesis using inductive logic programming for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus
finding: A hand-built object DSL as background knowledge plus ILP learns programs from few ARC examples, but only for a few tasks.
numbers: Solved 5 hand-picked sample tasks; no full-benchmark score reported.
limits: Selected tasks only; DSL coverage limits it. Authors say other tasks need other constructs.
agent_relevance: The old lesson: ILP is limited by background knowledge, which an LLM could propose.

source: Ai, Langer, Schmid and Muggleton (2026) Ultra strong machine learning: LLM-generated explanations do not yet suffice for teaching humans
finding: An ILP plus LLM pipeline produced explanations of learned strategies; an LLM judge rated them higher, but they did not help humans learn.
numbers: Human trial: 150 participants recruited (6 excluded); median split high baseline n=56, low baseline n=88. Expert-written explanations helped high-baseline learners; pipeline explanations gave no advantage over self-learning.
limits: Exploratory study; effect only in a subgroup; one interaction p=.021.
agent_relevance: LLM-judged quality did not predict outcomes. Never let an LLM judge approve a rule explanation; test with a real held-out check.
